business_problem: Explosive ordnance threats change over time, requiring detection methods that adapt to emerging threats and environments while helping EOD personnel locate munitions faster and avoid exposure to explosive hazards.
solution_summary: Dstl led a multi-week trial on behalf of the British Army with 33 Engineer Regiment (Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Search) at its Essex base. Dozens of replica mines and ordnance were placed across varied terrain and land environments to exercise the capability. Sensors onboard small uncrewed aerial systems captured data and relayed it to Army operators, who used AI tools to locate and identify the munitions. The trial demonstrated that AI models could be rapidly retrained for emerging threat types and adapted to different environments. The intended operational benefit is faster explosive-ordnance disposal work and reduced exposure of personnel to hazards. The release does not identify specific AI, sensor, communications, compute, or storage products, or describe data persistence. It says further trials will mature the technology and inform procurement of a deployable capability, so this is a trial rather than a reported fielded deployment.
data_flow: Sensors onboard small uncrewed aerial systems captured data and relayed it to Army operators, who used AI tools to locate and identify the munitions. The source does not describe storage or persistence.

Army operators, including 33 Engineer Regiment (EOD and Search) (AI-tool users)
business_outcome: The trial demonstrated a way for EOD operators to detect munitions faster, adapt models to changing threats and environments, and reduce personnel exposure to explosive hazards.
